restatements.text: Requires all county jails to hold individuals named in federal immigration detainer requests for up to 48 hours beyond their normal release time.

analysis.answer: Under current law, county officials have the discretion to honor or ignore federal immigration detainer requests. The measure removes this local discretion, mandating that every county jail honor the requests by holding individuals for up to 48 extra hours past their normal release time.

Counties face the direct cost of housing, feeding, and supervising individuals for up to an additional 48 hours. They may also face litigation costs and liability if holding individuals past their release date on an administrative detainer without a judicial warrant leads to civil rights lawsuits.

Federal immigration authorities benefit by securing a guaranteed window to take custody of individuals. County governments and local taxpayers bear the financial costs of the extended detention. The detained individuals bear the cost of extended loss of liberty.

Local law enforcement might alter arrest practices for minor offenses to manage jail populations or limit exposure to detainer mandates. Immigrant communities might become less willing to interact with local police, report crimes, or testify as witnesses due to the heightened risk of detention and deportation.

The measure addresses the issue of local jails releasing individuals sought by federal immigration authorities before those authorities can take custody. The mandate directly ensures individuals are held for transfer. However, it may create barriers to community policing by discouraging immigrants from cooperating with local law enforcement.

The state government and federal immigration authorities gain power. County governments and local jail administrators lose discretion over their detention policies, cooperation with federal agencies, and resource allocation.

The effect of local immigration cooperation on crime is disputed. Some researchers find that honoring detainers reduces crime by facilitating the removal of individuals who might reoffend, while others find it does not reduce crime and may harm overall public safety by depressing crime reporting within immigrant communities.
